items.title: Lionel Hampton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, October 18, 1995
items.q: I got Quincy Jones and he was making arrangements for the band

ctx.x: So your band was like a training ground for very many young musicians.

Yeah. And later down the line I got Quincy Jones, and I almost had Ray Charles, because Quincy Jones and Ray Charles were doing gigs together in Seattle, Washington. And I got Quincy Jones and he was making arrangements for the band, and then I picked up the piano player, what was his name, oh boy, Milt Buckner. Milt Buckner. You know he plays a lot of kinds of style of piano.
Yeah. He’s a good organist too.

items.title: Quincy Jones — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: INTERVIEWER mentions 'Hampton' in the context of 'Ghetto Gump' and volume matching; INTERVIEWEE responds 'That’s right' but discusses electric rhythm sections and Miles Davis, not a personal or professional relationship with Hampton.

ctx.x: If you say so – with Hampton made this so necessary, because with Fox Walker and Sonny Johnson – I had been told that a lot of this was because they had to have something that could match the volume.

That’s right. And that’s what happened, is it enabled the electric rhythm section – I mean, it became an electric rhythm section with the Fender bass, not the guitar, because it had no part – it had no allies. When that came, you say, yeah, I’ve been waiting for
